tracks.legalName: Petition to Close Nonconviction Court Records Entered Before 1 August 2025 (N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-05(2))
tracks.publicName: Close the court record of a North Dakota case that ended without a conviction

controllingAuthority.summary: Where an order of nonconviction was entered before 1 August 2025, the defendant may petition to close the court record, and the court shall enter the closing order within ten days of filing. A closed record may be examined only by the clerk, a judge, the juvenile commission, a criminal justice agency, the defendant, defence counsel, the state's attorney, or any person on the written order of a judge. Closing reaches the court record only: it does not close prosecutor or law enforcement records and does not reach BCI criminal history record information.

exclusions: A dismissal resulting from a plea agreement involving conviction on another offence.
A dismissal on a fitness-to-proceed finding under N.D.C.C. Chapter 12.1-04.
A verdict of not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility under N.D.C.C. Chapter 12.1-04.1.
Any case that was appealed.
Partial dispositions. Section 12-60.1-01(5) requires that all charges were dismissed or all acquitted.
Orders of nonconviction entered on or after 1 August 2025, which close automatically and need no petition.

rules.researchProductMechanismVersusLaw: The nonfiled clerk-correction request is a proposed administrative step; the five-business-day interval after confirmed receipt is an optional LegalEase cure interval, not a statutory prerequisite, and an express refusal or an instruction to seek a judicial order may allow the product to advance earlier. The statute prescribes no letter, interval or specially named enforcement motion; counsel or design adoption is still required for the custom escalation strategy. The proposed escalation is a motion in the original case requesting performance of the statutory closing duty, not a discretionary conviction-sealing petition or an appellate challenge; relief is restricted to court-controlled records and never promises removal of prosecutor, police, federal or private database records.
rules.researchEnforcementPacket: An approved enforcement design includes the original caption, the motion, a notice of motion and short supporting brief (N.D.R.Ct. 3.2 requires notice and a brief; its note allows a liberal understanding of what constitutes a brief; a concise legal-grounds section suffices), a factual declaration and exhibits where needed, a proposed order, and proof of service. N.D.R.Crim.P. 47(c) generally requires a written motion and hearing notice at least 21 days before a hearing unless another rule or court order sets a different time; no automatic 21-day delay is hardcoded for a motion submitted on briefs and the five-day administrative interval never satisfies hearing notice. Rule 3.2 supplies a 14-day answer-brief period and a seven-day reply period and allows a hearing request. Rule 49 requires service on the other parties, ordinarily through the prosecuting attorney, by permitted methods with proof filed. The official six-page packet (Rev. April 2026) is principally the petition and order package for pre-August-2025 nonconvictions; its earlier-case petition is never populated as the post-period letter and its note about a judge possibly requiring a prosecutor copy is not imported into the Rule 49 motion.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Seal a Misdemeanor Conviction (N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-02(1)(a))
tracks.publicName: Ask a North Dakota court to seal a misdemeanor conviction

controllingAuthority.summary: A person who pled guilty to or was found guilty of a misdemeanor may petition to seal the record if they have not been convicted of a new crime for at least three years before filing the petition. Sealing prohibits disclosure of the existence or contents of court and prosecution records except by court order. The three years are a look-back from filing, not a wait measured from sentence completion; completion of imprisonment and probation and payment of restitution are separate findings the court must make under § 12-60.1-04(1)(c) and (d).

exclusions: Any offence for which the offender has been ordered to register under N.D.C.C. § 12.1-32-15.
Impaired-driving offences, which the official guides route to the separate seal under N.D.C.C. § 39-08-01.6.

waitingPeriods.condition: No conviction of a new crime in the look-back period
waitingPeriods.duration: three years immediately before the petition is filed
all terms of imprisonment and probation complete and all restitution paid; these are findings rather than waiting periods

geography.venue: The existing criminal case for the offence, under N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-03(1). There is no separate civil action. District court or municipal court, whichever holds the case.

destination.name: Clerk of Court of the existing criminal case
destination.detail: Filed in the criminal case itself. The respondent is the prosecuting attorney: the office of the prosecuting official for the municipality in a municipal case, or the office of the State's Attorney for the county in a district court case. The petitioner serves the prosecuting attorney under N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-03(4), which routes through N.D.R.Crim.P. 49 to N.D.R.Civ.P. 5(b).

rules.filing: Serve the prosecuting attorney, then file the petition, the mandatory proposed order and the proof of service with the clerk of the criminal case.
rules.fees: Not established. The statewide court fee schedule effective 1 July 2025 carries no line item for a Chapter 12-60.1 petition or for a motion within an existing criminal case, and the official research guide directs the participant to ask the clerk what the fee is, if any.
rules.feeWaiver: Not established for this petition. N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-04(6) expressly makes a municipal-to-district-court appeal fee-free, which implies a fee may attach at first instance.
rules.notice: The prosecutor must, so far as practicable, notify and seek input from law enforcement, witnesses, victims and correctional authorities under N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-04(4).
rules.service: On the prosecuting attorney, under N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-03(4) through N.D.R.Crim.P. 49 and N.D.R.Civ.P. 5(b). The participant serves and files proof.
rules.participantSignature: The petitioner signs the petition. N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-03 imposes no verification requirement, so no sworn form of signature is required.
rules.notarization: none required. The chapter contains no verification clause.

components.notes: Petition to Seal Criminal Records Under N.D.C.C. Chapter 12-60.1, captioned in the existing criminal case. Contents follow N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-03(2)(a) to (d): the petitioner's identity and every other name used, the address history from the offence to filing, the reasons sealing should be granted, and the full criminal history including out-of-state, federal and foreign matters and every prior relief request in any forum. Subject to the redaction requirements of N.D.R.Ct. 3.4.

Proposed Order to Seal Criminal Records. N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-03(3) makes this mandatory: the petitioner shall file a proposed order when filing the petition. It must recite the six findings in § 12-60.1-04(1) and the § 12-60.1-04(8) language that the petitioner is sufficiently rehabilitated but remains subject to N.D.C.C. § 12.1-33-02.1 and that the information is released where an entity has a statutory obligation to conduct a criminal history background check.
Affidavit or declaration of service on the prosecuting attorney, or a certificate of service where a sheriff served. The official research guide supplies the Rule 5(b) declarations.

tracks.publicName: Clear a North Dakota case where the court deferred your sentence

controllingAuthority.summary: N.D.R.Crim.P. 32.1 makes it a mandatory term of every order deferring imposition of sentence that, sixty-one days after probation expires or terminates, the guilty plea is withdrawn or the verdict set aside, the case is dismissed and the file is sealed. Since the amendment effective 1 March 2019 the rule applies in all cases, not only misdemeanors and infractions. Where the term did not operate, the defendant may move under N.D.C.C. § 12.1-32-07.1, which also permits the court, on application by the defendant, to reduce a felony to a misdemeanor before dismissing. A deferred disposition remains pleadable in a later prosecution under § 12.1-32-02(4) and counts as a conviction for firearm purposes under § 62.1-02-01(2).

exclusions: A petition for revocation filed within sixty days of expiration or termination of probation.
An outstanding bench warrant in the deferred matter.
Registration consequences under N.D.C.C. § 12.1-32-15 and firearm consequences under § 62.1-02-01, both of which survive dismissal.

tracks.legalName: Routing of Expungement of Records of an Unconstitutional Arrest (State v. Howe, 308 N.W.2d 743 (N.D. 1981))
tracks.publicName: Where to go if you believe your arrest was unconstitutional

controllingAuthority.summary: Where an arrest was unconstitutional and the charges were dismissed or the conviction overturned, the defendant may petition the court to expunge the arrest records. The official ND Legal Self Help Center expungement guide identifies State v. Howe as the source of this route and lists it as one of North Dakota's expungement mechanisms. There is no North Dakota Century Code section for it.

exclusions: Any case where the conviction stands.
Any case where no constitutional defect in the arrest is asserted.

geography.venue: The court where the arrest record originates.

destination.name: No destination. This node routes rather than files
destination.detail: The node routes to counsel. A participant-facing petition exists according to the official guide and no official form is published, but the controlling authority cannot be obtained from any official electronic source, so the route is not built.

components.notes: Explains that the route exists, that it is a true expungement rather than sealing, that it rests on a 1981 Supreme Court decision rather than a statute, and that the standard cannot be stated from an official electronic source. Routes to counsel and generates nothing.

participantInputs.question: On what date were you arrested?
